summary: Children aged 9–11 learn that an irreversible change forms a NEW material with different properties, and the original materials usually cannot easily be got back. The core teaching move is judging change by EVIDENCE of a new substance — fizz/gas, colour change, heat or light given off, a smell, or a new solid — remembering that one sign alone is not proof, and by experiencing a failed attempt to reverse it. Canonical examples (from UK DfE Y5 and matched to NGSS 5-PS1-4) are burning and acid on bicarbonate of soda, extended with rusting and cooking. Learners contrast these directly with reversible changes. Keep the point that matter is not destroyed (gases carry mass away) honest but light, and leave formal conservation in reactions for later.
misconceptions: All changes can be reversed if you try hard enough.
Burning destroys matter completely (missing that gases and ash carry the mass).
A colour change alone is not 'really' a new substance.
Cooking is just heating/melting rather than forming new materials.
Rusting is dirt on the surface rather than a new substance formed from the iron.

activities.title: New-substance detector bench with failed reversals
steps: Trigger a change at each station: pour vinegar onto bicarbonate of soda and watch it froth; move a time-lapse slider so a shiny nail blooms orange then crumbles to rust; observe a guarded flame turn white paper into blackened char, grey ash and smoke (burning kept as a supervised teacher demonstration — learners observe, they do not ignite anything).

For each change, fill in an evidence-of-new-substance checklist: gas/fizz? colour change? heat or light given off? smell? new solid? (Expect different changes to show different signs — e.g. vinegar+bicarb shows gas but no heat, while burning gives off heat and light.)

Try a simple reversal for each change (e.g. cooling, drying, scraping or sieving; for simulated stations, a 'reverse' control) and record that it does not bring back the originals — e.g. a stamp reading 'can't undo: a new substance was made (here, a gas)'. Remember that a simulated control only shows the result someone programmed; the real evidence is the signs you observed.

Compare side by side with a reversible change (melting chocolate that sets again when cooled) and state the rule in your own words: when the signs show a new material formed, the change usually can't easily be reversed.
activities.insight: Irreversibility is detected by evidence that a new substance formed, and experienced through reversal attempts that fail — not memorised as a definition.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: the balloon and the bottle
steps: Before mixing, predict what a balloon stretched over a bottle containing a little baking soda will do when vinegar is tipped in — and say WHY.
Tip in the vinegar, observe the balloon inflate, and explain what the gas tells you about whether a new substance was made.

Answer probing questions: burning toast, a firework, and rusting iron — what sign in each shows a new substance formed? If nothing was heated, why did a gas appear? How is this different from stirring sand into salt, which you CAN separate again? If someone says 'it's just hidden, not changed', what evidence shows it is really new?
activities.insight: A gas appearing with no heating is strong evidence of a newly-made substance, which distinguishes an irreversible chemical change from mere mixing or boiling.

activities.title: Sort and match: reversible vs irreversible by its sign
steps: Sort a set of changes into reversible and irreversible, explaining the reason for each.

For each irreversible change, match it to the evidence-of-new-substance sign that justifies the classification (e.g. acid+bicarb → gas produced; rusting → new solid / colour change; burning → heat/light given off + ash as a new solid).
Contrast a genuine mixture (sand stirred into salt, separable) with a change that made a new substance, and state why one can be undone and the other cannot.
activities.insight: Classifying a change requires justification by an observed sign, not just a label — and a separable mixture is not an irreversible change.

activities.title: Example gallery of irreversible changes
steps: Review a panel of irreversible changes (burning, rusting, acid+bicarb, cooking an egg or cake), revealing the new-substance sign(s) for each.
For each example, say in your own words what the original material was, what new material formed, and which sign gives it away.
activities.insight: A wider set of worked examples reinforces the general test: different changes, same category because each shows evidence of a new material.

checkQuestion: When we mixed vinegar with baking soda it fizzed and bubbled up, and the fizzing left something that is NOT vinegar and NOT baking soda any more. How can you tell a NEW substance was made — what were the signs? And could you get your vinegar and baking soda back?
checkAnswer: You can tell a new substance formed by the signs: a gas was made (fizzing/bubbles), and things can also change colour, give off heat or light, or leave a new solid. No — you can't get the original vinegar and baking soda back; that's what makes it irreversible: a new substance has been made, so it can't run backwards.
